serviceDescription: This is a simplified high resolution set of coastal polygons used for extracting offshore and SF Bay open water areas out of other polygons. It is based on NOAA's Continually Updated Shoreline Product (CUSP) as of September 2024. Its primary purpose is to remove coastal buffers from polygons using a relatively accurate shoreline, but is not accurate enough to be used in regulatory decisionmaking or parcel/property-level analysis due to the nature of the modifications we made to NOAA's data.
description:
This dataset was produced to remove coastal buffers, so it strives to keep ocean-facing shoreline intact, remove estuaries and marsh channels (considering those to be land-side), enclose large harbors where commercial activity may happen, and remove protrusions like breakwaters when they aren't designed for human occupation (e.g. no paths along them). For this purpose, we utilized the Esri satellite basemap and CDT"s 2022 Hexagon imagery to review the coastline data.

This dataset was produced in order to aid in removal of coastal buffers from the boundaries of cities and counties in California"s official boundary data for the purposes of visualizing and calculating the approximate land-based areas. The decisions made on what to include and exclude from the coastline are influenced by that purpose, and may not suit all needs.

This dataset also aims to align with some existing datasets of city and county boundaries, which results in the incorporation of the San Francisco Bay as water, but the enclosing of San Diego and Humboldt Bays. While San Francisco Bay is included as water, it is tagged as a “bay” in the COASTAL field, while offshore locations are tagged as “ocean”. We use this to make differing cuts to different datasets.

The boundaries are cartographic in that they have no regulatory meaning, but they are based on modified high-resolution shoreline data from NOAA and are accurate to very large scales.

Usage

These data are polygon so that they can be used to both cut and tag (via a Union operation) other polygon datasets. That operation also means that, even though these are not regulatory polygons, they can split regulatory boundaries like cities or counties at the coastline while preserving the existing polygons with additional tagging to know what is offshore. The polygon boundary extends north and south of the state a small amount and then out into the ocean far enough to capture all islands for this purpose.

In our internal usage, we do significant postprocessing to remove slivers created by the union operation. Sliver processing will vary, but our algorithm restores the original boundary of the other dataset where it closely aligns with the coastline dataset.

Modifications

In determining which parts of the coastline to include, we followed the following rough guidelines, though many places remain a judgement call - these are not hard and fast rules. The goal is to make a relatively internally consistent product, but not necessarily one that will meet all uses.

  • Estuaries and marshes: Closed off, typically at a location close to where the channel narrows, so part of the inlet may remain
  • Breakwaters and walls: Removed wherever the last piece of human occupiable infrastructure ends (e.g. end of a road, path, or pier) before rocks or other wall begin
  • Harbors: Enclosed when mostly surrounded by land, left open otherwise.

In the San Francisco Bay, this dataset extends inland to the edge of Sacramento and Contra Coast counties, following the Solano and Contra Costa county lines over the water.

In many cases, decisions were a judgement call more than a science - we welcome feedback on what should be included or excluded.
